conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from internal medicine. I understand you've been having a lot of nausea and vomiting since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. Started with nausea at breakfast, then couldn’t keep anything down. Diarrhea got really bad too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any abdominal pain, fever, or chest discomfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain. Had chills overnight, but no fever I checked. Felt short of breath when I arrived, but it passed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll monitor that. I see you’re on a lot of medications—especially for your liver transplant and chronic nausea. You’ve stopped eating and G-tube feeds because of the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, couldn’t keep anything down. I use the G-tube most days, but I’ve been using it less since the nausea started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. Your labs show your kidney function is worse than usual—creatinine is 2.3, normally around 1.5. This is likely from dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, but likely reversible. We’re giving IV fluids to help. Your FeNa is low, which means your kidneys are trying to hold onto water—so it’s pre-renal, not permanent damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you Zofran in the ER. We’ll continue that and add lorazepam, which can help with nausea, especially in patients like you with a history of intractable symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve used that before. Helps a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also did a chest X-ray. You have a moderate right pleural effusion—fluid around the lung. It’s slightly worse than before, but no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that for a while. My liver team said it’s from my liver disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s common after transplant. We’ll keep an eye on it, but it’s not the cause of your current symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s causing the nausea and diarrhea then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely a viral gastroenteritis—maybe norovirus. You’re immunosuppressed, so we’re checking stool for parasites and bacteria, but so far everything’s negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had C. diff before. Could it be that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested for C. diff—it’s negative. So not that. We’ve held your opium tincture for now until we’re sure it’s not infectious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need that for the diarrhea. It’s constant otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Once we confirm it’s not infectious, we’ll restart it. For now, we’re focusing on hydration and letting your gut rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool tests all came back negative—no bacteria, parasites, or viruses detected. That supports a viral cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s probably just a stomach bug?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Given your transplant and immunosuppression, we had to be cautious. But now we can safely restart your opium tincture for the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been wearing diapers for years because of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing it. Your kidney function is already improving—creatinine down to 1.9. IV fluids are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I try some food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small amounts—soft foods, low lactose. No G-tube feeds yet. We want to see how you tolerate eating by mouth first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You kept down breakfast and lunch yesterday. Creatinine is now 1.8. We’re slowing the IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel weak, but the nausea is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. You lost a lot of fluid. We gave you a unit of blood yesterday—your hemoglobin was low at 9.8, so you’re anemic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get those darbepoetin shots every two weeks. They help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue those. Your pain seems better too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still some back and neck pain, but I’ve had that for years. Dilaudid helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your pain meds as needed. One thing—we’re adjusting your gabapentin. You were on 600 mg twice daily, but we’re reducing it to 300 mg once daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why? It helps with the nerve pain from the shingles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re simplifying your meds. The lower dose is still effective for maintenance, and it’s safer with your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your creatinine is now 1.7, back toward your baseline. You’ve had no vomiting in 24 hours and your diarrhea is back to your usual chronic level.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Planning to discharge tomorrow. We’ll send you home with oral Zofran for nausea—4 mg three times a day for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had Zofran before. Helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And you’ll restart your G-tube feeds as needed. High-fiber, low-lactose diet to help with bowel control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can handle that. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual meds continue—Cellcept, prednisone, Valcylovir for shingles, fludrocortisone, and the rest. No changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another rejection scare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are normal, so no sign of rejection. You’re doing well with the transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my PCP and liver team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Drink at least four glasses of water daily, keep using the G-tube as needed, and call if nausea returns or you can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for restarting the opium tincture. It makes a big difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. It’s safe now that we’ve ruled out infection. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. You’ll go home with a wheelchair for support, but you’re still independent with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I use it when I get tired. Walker’s fine for short distances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And keep up with your follow-ups—especially for the cervical hardware erosion and your skin sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had issues with the hardware lately. The sore on my back is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Just stay vigilant. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay hydrated.
